MUQATIL:89:23-26/r1.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:89:23-26/r1.speaker: author
MUQATIL:89:23-26/r1.claim: Hell is brought from a distance of 500 years with 70,000 reins and 70,000 angels on each; their fearsome eyes, fiery mouths, mountain-sized maces, and seven snake-like heads show its rage against creatures.

MUQATIL:89:23-26/r2.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:89:23-26/r2.speaker: author
MUQATIL:89:23-26/r2.claim: The angels restrain Hell from the creatures until it is set upright before them.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p371#3/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p371#3/r1.speaker: أبو وائل
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p371#3/r1.claim: Abu Wa'il says Hell is brought in with a muzzle or bridle.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p371#3/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p371#3/r2.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p371#3/r2.claim: Abdullah ibn Amr describes seven seas of fire and seven seas of water beneath the sea people know.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p371#3/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p371#3/r3.speaker: سعيد بن أبي الحسن
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p371#3/r3.claim: Sa'id ibn Abi al-Hasan says the sea is a covering layer over Hell.

TAB-FULL:v24p390#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p390#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v24p390#2/r1.claim: On that day a person recalls his neglect in worldly obedience to God and good works, but is too late to benefit from the reminder.

TAB-FULL:v24p390#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p390#2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v24p390#2/r2.claim: He explains the question as asking how remembrance can help the person then.

TAB-FULL:v24p390/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p390/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v24p390/r1.claim: God brings Hell on Judgment Day.

TAB-FULL:v24p390/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p390/r2.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود، أبو وائل
TAB-FULL:v24p390/r2.claim: Hell is brought led by seventy thousand reins, each held by seventy thousand angels.

TAB-FULL:v24p390/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p390/r3.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v24p390/r3.claim: He describes Paradise and the Fire at the two sides, and says this is when God descends from His Throne to His Footstool to judge creation.

ZAJJAJ:v5p323/r4.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p323/r4.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p323/r4.claim: Hell is brought forth, as in the statement that it was exposed to the sinners; tafsīr says it is dragged by a million reins, each held by seventy thousand angels.

ZAJJAJ:v5p323/r5.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p323/r5.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p323/r5.claim: On that day people display repentance; “how could he remember?” means “how could he repent then?”

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3429#3/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3429#3/r1.speaker: الضحاك
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3429#3/r1.claim: Al-Dahhak says the person remembers and seeks repentance.

NAHHAS:v5p223/r10.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p223/r10.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v5p223/r10.claim: Assimilating the tāʾ into dhāl in yatadhakkaru is permissible.

NAHHAS:v5p223/r12.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p223/r12.speaker: قيل
NAHHAS:v5p223/r12.claim: Another interpretation asks how remembrance could benefit the person at that point.

NAHHAS:v5p223/r9.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p223/r9.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v5p223/r9.claim: The opening verb is passive, with the following noun in the deputy-subject position; alternatively, it may be a verbal noun.

THALABI:v10p201/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p201/r4.speaker: أبو سعيد عن النبي
THALABI:v10p201/r4.claim: When this verse was revealed, the Prophet became pale and sweated; Gabriel recited the passage, and Hell is brought by seventy thousand angels with seventy thousand reins, charges toward the assembly, then says Muhammad's flesh and blood are forbidden to it. Everyone pleads for himself while Muhammad pleads for his community.

THALABI:v10p202/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p202/r1.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود ومقاتل
THALABI:v10p202/r1.claim: They say Hell is led by seventy thousand reins, each held by seventy thousand angels, and roars until it is set to the left of the Throne.

THALABI:v10p202/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p202/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p202/r2.claim: On that day a person remembers and wishes he had sent deeds ahead for his afterlife, but remembrance then comes too late.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p271/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p271/r1.speaker: الضحاك
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p271/r1.claim: Remembering on that day may mean repentance, but repentance at the Resurrection can no longer benefit a person.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p271/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p271/r2.speaker: ابن شجرة
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p271/r2.claim: It may mean recalling one's worldly deeds and what one sent ahead for the afterlife, a benefit available only in worldly life.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p520/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p520/r4.speaker: جماعة المفسرين
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p520/r4.claim: Hell is brought bound with 70,000 reins, each held by 70,000 angels, until it stands to the left of the Throne.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p520/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p520/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p520/r5.claim: The second yawm idhin refers to the day Hell is brought, and the human's remembering means the disbeliever takes admonition and repents.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p521/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p521/r1.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v23p521/r1.claim: He understands anna lahu al-dhikra as asking how repentance could be available then; he links the wording to a similar question about the messenger's arrival.

WAHIDI-QT:89:23/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-QT:89:23/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-QT:89:23/r1.claim: Hell is brought forward with seventy thousand reins, each held by seventy thousand angels.

WAHIDI-QT:89:23/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-QT:89:23/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-QT:89:23/r2.claim: On that day the unbeliever shows repentance, but the question means there is no way for him to repent then.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:89:18-25/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:89:18-25/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:89:18-25/r4.claim: Hell is brought on seventy thousand reins, each held by seventy thousand angels; the disbeliever manifests repentance, but it is too late.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p422#2/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p422#2/r4.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود ومقاتل
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p422#2/r4.claim: Ibn Masud and Muqatil report that Hell is led by 70,000 reins, each held by 70,000 angels, roaring until set to the Throne’s left.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p422#2/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p422#2/r5.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p422#2/r5.claim: ‘That day’ means the day Hell is brought; the unbeliever takes warning and repents, but, al-Zajjaj asks, how can repentance help then?

KASHSHAF:89:23/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:89:23/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:89:23/r1.claim: Bringing Hell is comparable to the verse saying that Hell is exposed.

KASHSHAF:89:23/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:89:23/r2.speaker: النبي
KASHSHAF:89:23/r2.claim: A report says this verse changed the Prophet's face; when Ali asked how Hell would be brought, the Prophet said 70,000 angels would lead it on 70,000 reins, and it could break loose and burn the assembly; no grading is stated.

KASHSHAF:89:23/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:89:23/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:89:23/r3.claim: The human remembers what he neglected, or takes warning from it.

KASHSHAF:89:23/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:89:23/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:89:23/r4.claim: The question means that remembrance will not benefit him; an omitted genitive must be supplied, or the paired clauses would conflict.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p480#3/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p480#3/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p480#3/r1.claim: A report says Hell is brought with seventy thousand reins, each held by seventy thousand angels, and a neck selects tyrannical disbelievers; wording varies.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p480#3/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p480#3/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p480#3/r2.claim: Here Hell means the whole Fire.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p480#3/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p480#3/r3.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p480#3/r3.claim: A report says the Prophet's color changed when this verse was revealed.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p480#3/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p480#3/r4.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p480#3/r4.claim: On that day a person recalls disobedience and transgression and sees the good deeds he missed.

TABRISI:89:1-30#10/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:89:1-30#10/r1.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
TABRISI:89:1-30#10/r1.claim: The Prophet reportedly tells Ali that Gabriel recited the verse about Hell being brought on Judgment Day.

TABRISI:89:1-30#10/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:89:1-30#10/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:89:1-30#10/r2.claim: The event makes people remember and repent, but the author asks rhetorically where repentance can now come from.

TABRISI:89:1-30#10/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:89:1-30#10/r3.speaker: الزجاج
TABRISI:89:1-30#10/r3.claim: Al-Zajjaj glosses the question as “from where could he get repentance?”

TABRISI:89:1-30#10/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:89:1-30#10/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:89:1-30#10/r4.claim: An alternative says the person remembers his failures once God's warning is certain but receives no benefit from remembering then.

TABRISI:89:1-30#9/r10.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:89:1-30#9/r10.speaker: author
TABRISI:89:1-30#9/r10.claim: Hell is brought forward so the deserving can be punished and everyone present can witness its terrifying magnitude.

TABRISI:89:1-30#9/r11.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:89:1-30#9/r11.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
TABRISI:89:1-30#9/r11.claim: A Prophetic report says Gabriel recited the verse; Hell is led by 70,000 angels holding 70,000 reins, bolts to burn the assembly, rejects Muhammad's flesh, and leaves everyone pleading for himself while Muhammad pleads for his community.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p121#4/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p121#4/r1.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p121#4/r1.claim: A report in Muslim says Hell will be brought with 70,000 reins, each pulled by 70,000 angels.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p121#4/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p121#4/r2.speaker: مقاتل
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p121#4/r2.claim: Hell will be brought and positioned to the left of the Throne.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p121#4/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p121#4/r3.speaker: مقاتل
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p121#4/r3.claim: The unbeliever remembers, takes warning, and repents on that Day, but repentance cannot benefit him in the Resurrection.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p121#4/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p121#4/r4.speaker: مقاتل
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p121#4/r4.claim: The human mentioned here is Umayya ibn Khalaf; repentance in the Resurrection is too late.

RAZI:89:23/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:89:23/r1.speaker: جماعة من المفسرين
RAZI:89:23/r1.claim: A group says Hell will be brought at Resurrection bound with seventy thousand reins, each pulled by seventy thousand angels; it will strain as if to escape and would burn the gathering if released.

RAZI:89:23/r10.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:89:23/r10.speaker: author
RAZI:89:23/r10.claim: His argument is that people recognize their worldly choices were wrong and regret them, thereby repenting, yet the verse denies that this repentance benefits them.

RAZI:89:23/r11.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:89:23/r11.speaker: author
RAZI:89:23/r11.claim: An objection says their regret was only fear of punishment, not regret for wrongdoing, so it was not valid repentance; the author replies that useful regret must be for the wrongness itself, making it valid repentance despite nonacceptance.

RAZI:89:23/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:89:23/r2.speaker: الأصوليون
RAZI:89:23/r2.claim: The theologians say Hell does not leave its place; being brought forth means being exposed so creation sees it and the unbeliever recognizes his destination.

RAZI:89:23/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:89:23/r3.speaker: author
RAZI:89:23/r3.claim: The syntax supplies a temporal condition: when the earth is crushed and the other events occur, then that day the human remembers.

RAZI:89:23/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:89:23/r4.speaker: author
RAZI:89:23/r4.claim: One explanation is that a person recalls having wrongly devoted worldly effort to this life instead of making the afterlife the goal.

RAZI:89:23/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:89:23/r5.speaker: author
RAZI:89:23/r5.claim: A second explanation makes يتذكر mean taking heed: those who ignored admonition in worldly life become admonished in the next and wish to return.

RAZI:89:23/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:89:23/r6.speaker: الحسن
RAZI:89:23/r6.claim: Al-Hasan is reported to interpret the remembering as repentance.

RAZI:89:23/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:89:23/r7.speaker: author
RAZI:89:23/r7.claim: The apparent contradiction between remembering and the question how remembrance could help is resolved by supplying “benefit”: how could he benefit from remembrance then?

RAZI:89:23/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:89:23/r8.speaker: author
RAZI:89:23/r8.claim: The author holds that accepting repentance is not rationally obligatory for God; the verse says the sinner’s eventual repentance will not benefit him.

RAZI:89:23/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:89:23/r9.speaker: المعتزلة
RAZI:89:23/r9.claim: The Muʿtazilites maintain that accepting repentance is rationally obligatory.

QURTUBI-FULL:89:22-23#2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:89:22-23#2/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:89:22-23#2/r1.claim: The human remembers by taking warning and repenting; the person may be an unbeliever or someone absorbed in worldly life.

QURTUBI-FULL:89:22-23#2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:89:22-23#2/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:89:22-23#2/r2.claim: The rhetorical question asks how remembrance could help after it was neglected in worldly life, or where its benefit could come from.

QURTUBI-FULL:89:22-23#2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:89:22-23#2/r3.speaker: الزمخشري
QURTUBI-FULL:89:22-23#2/r3.claim: He says an implied noun must be supplied to avoid contradiction between remembering and asking how remembrance is possible.

QURTUBI-FULL:89:22-23/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:89:22-23/r6.speaker: ابن مسعود ومقاتل
QURTUBI-FULL:89:22-23/r6.claim: Hell is dragged by 70,000 bridles, each held by 70,000 angels, roaring until it is stationed left of the Throne.

QURTUBI-FULL:89:22-23/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:89:22-23/r7.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود عن النبي
QURTUBI-FULL:89:22-23/r7.claim: A sound Muslim report repeats that Hell will arrive with 70,000 bridles, each accompanied by 70,000 angels pulling it.

QURTUBI-FULL:89:22-23/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:89:22-23/r8.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري عن النبي
QURTUBI-FULL:89:22-23/r8.claim: When the verse was revealed, the Prophet's color changed; Gabriel recited it to him, and the companions saw his distress.

QURTUBI-FULL:89:22-23/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:89:22-23/r9.speaker: علي عن النبي
QURTUBI-FULL:89:22-23/r9.claim: Hell is led on 70,000 bridles and would burn the assembled people if allowed to escape; it addresses Muhammad, whom God has protected from it.

BAYDAWI-FULL:89:20-25/r6.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:89:20-25/r6.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:89:20-25/r6.claim: Hell is brought forward, as in 26:91; a report depicts seventy thousand reins, each led by seventy thousand angels.

BAYDAWI-FULL:89:20-25/r7.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:89:20-25/r7.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
BAYDAWI-FULL:89:20-25/r7.claim: The Prophet reports that Hell arrives with seventy thousand reins, each pulled by seventy thousand angels; no grading is stated.

BAYDAWI-FULL:89:20-25/r8.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:89:20-25/r8.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:89:20-25/r8.claim: The human recalls sins or takes heed and regrets them, but that remembrance cannot benefit; this wording has been used to argue repentance need not be accepted at that time.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p338#6/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p338#6/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p338#6/r1.claim: Hell may be brought forth visibly, as in the verse about it being exposed to the straying, or literally brought on the Day; a report describes seventy thousand reins, each drawn by seventy thousand angels.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p338#6/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p338#6/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p338#6/r2.claim: The person will take heed then, but the remembrance can no longer benefit him.

QASHANI:89:21-23/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:89:21-23/r2.speaker: author
QASHANI:89:21-23/r2.claim: Hell is exposed as the fire of nature and brought for those punished.

QASHANI:89:21-23/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:89:21-23/r3.speaker: author
QASHANI:89:21-23/r3.claim: People then recall beliefs contrary to reality, but this reminder cannot help because entrenched belief blocks its benefit.

SAMIN-DURR:89:23/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:89:23/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:89:23/r1.claim: The first ‘yawma’ is governed by ‘ji’a’ and ‘bi-jahannam’ is its passive deputy; Makki also allows the day expression itself to be the passive deputy.

SAMIN-DURR:89:23/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:89:23/r2.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:89:23/r2.claim: The second ‘yawma’ may substitute for ‘idha dukkat’; on the Sibawayh approach it shares that phrase’s governor, whereas others understand the governor as repeated.

SAMIN-DURR:89:23/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:89:23/r3.speaker: أبو البقاء
SAMIN-DURR:89:23/r3.claim: Abu al-Baqa assigns ‘yaqulu’ as governor of ‘idha dukkat’ and ‘yatadhakkar’ as governor of the second ‘yawma’.

SAMIN-DURR:89:23/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:89:23/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:89:23/r4.claim: In ‘wa-anna lahu al-dhikra’, ‘anna’ is a fronted predicate, ‘al-dhikra’ its delayed subject, and ‘lahu’ attaches to the predicate.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p399#3/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p399#3/r1.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p399#3/r1.claim: The Prophet says Hell will be brought with seventy thousand reins, each pulled by seventy thousand angels; Ibn Kathir cites the report in Muslim and notes parallel versions attributed to Ibn Masud.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p399#3/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p399#3/r2.speaker: ابن جرير
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p399#3/r2.claim: Ibn Jarir also transmits the description as Abd Allah ibn Masud's own statement, not as a Prophetic report.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p400/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p400/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p400/r1.claim: On that day a person recalls earlier and recent deeds, but the reminder comes too late to help.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p421/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p421/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p421/r1.claim: Hell does not arrive by itself, which might suggest it lies beyond God’s power; angels drag it, and its arrival itself creates overwhelming terror.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p421/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p421/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p421/r2.claim: An unattributed report says Hell will be brought with seventy thousand reins, each accompanied by seventy thousand angels.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p421/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p421/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p421/r3.claim: The passive wording focuses on the terrifying act of bringing Hell rather than identifying those who bring it; it recalls the verse that Hell is exposed to view.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p422/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p422/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p422/r1.claim: The repeated yawm idh clarifies the earlier time marker after a long interruption and magnifies the terror of seeing what awaits the grateful and unbelieving.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p422/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p422/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p422/r2.claim: Humanity then remembers what helped or harmed in worldly life and sees that attachment to the world brought only loss; remembrance cannot help because the time for action has passed.

DURR-FULL:v8p511/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p511/r8.speaker: أبو سعيد
DURR-FULL:v8p511/r8.claim: At the verse's revelation the Prophet looked distressed; Gabriel described Hell led by 70,000 angels holding 70,000 reins, and said it would burn the assembly if it broke loose.

DURR-FULL:v8p512/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p512/r1.speaker: زيد بن أسلم عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
DURR-FULL:v8p512/r1.claim: Gabriel told the Prophet that Hell would be brought on 70,000 reins, each led by 70,000 angels; it once broke free but was caught before burning the gathering.

DURR-FULL:v8p512/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p512/r2.speaker: ابن مسعود
DURR-FULL:v8p512/r2.claim: The Prophet said Hell will arrive with 70,000 reins, each accompanied by 70,000 angels pulling it.

DURR-FULL:v8p512/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p512/r3.speaker: ابن مسعود
DURR-FULL:v8p512/r3.claim: He explained that Hell is led by 70,000 reins, each guided by 70,000 angels.

DURR-FULL:v8p512/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p512/r4.speaker: الضحاك
DURR-FULL:v8p512/r4.claim: He said the human remembers and seeks repentance; ‘I wish I had prepared for my life’ means preparing in this world for the afterlife.

DURR-FULL:v8p512/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p512/r5.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v8p512/r5.claim: He said the person then knows the truth: the afterlife is a long, deathless life better than this one.

BURSEVI:v10p332#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p332#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p332#2/r1.claim: Hell need not be brought metaphorically: places can be brought in an instant by origination and annihilation; the expanded earth can contain Hell and the assembly, and its imaginal form may also appear, like Jerusalem shown to the Prophet.

BURSEVI:v10p332#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p332#2/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p332#2/r2.claim: The person remembers failures by seeing their effects or embodied deeds, or finally accepts worldly guidance; the resulting regret is like repentance, but it is too late to benefit.

BURSEVI:v10p332#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p332#2/r3.speaker: القاشاني
BURSEVI:v10p332#2/r3.claim: Al-Qashani says people then realize the truth contradicted their worldly beliefs: God appears in majesty and angels in the punishment their denial had earned.

BURSEVI:v10p332#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p332#2/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p332#2/r4.claim: The inserted question “how can remembrance help?” establishes that recollection and repentance after their proper time have no benefit.

BURSEVI:v10p332#2/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p332#2/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p332#2/r5.claim: Bursevi argues that late repentance not being accepted shows there is no rational obligation to accept repentance; he then quotes al-Irshad’s objection that the verse proves nothing about repentance during earthly life and this recollection is not true repentance.

BURSEVI:v10p332#2/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p332#2/r6.speaker: الإرشاد
BURSEVI:v10p332#2/r6.claim: Al-Irshad rejects that inference about repentance during worldly life: the remembered event is not repentance, since the person knows repentance must occur before death.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p128#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p128#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p128#2/r1.claim: “Hell is brought” might mean that it is displayed, but Alusi prefers a literal bringing because its movement from its place in the gathering is not impossible.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p128#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p128#2/r2.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
ALUSI-FULL:v30p128#2/r2.claim: Ibn Masʿud reports from the Prophet that Hell is brought with 70,000 reins, each led by 70,000 angels; the report appears in Muslim, Tirmidhi, and other collections.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p128#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p128#2/r3.speaker: علي
ALUSI-FULL:v30p128#2/r3.claim: In a report about Gabriel's visit, Ali asks how Hell will be brought; the Prophet describes 70,000 reins with 70,000 angels each, and says that without their catching it, it would have burned the gathered people or the heavens and earth.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p128#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p128#2/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p128#2/r4.claim: “That day” is an appositive for the time when the earth is crushed; although al-Zamakhshari appears to make the same verb govern both clauses, the apparent stronger analysis repeats the governing word for the appositive.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p128#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p128#2/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p128#2/r5.claim: The person remembers his failures in detail through seeing their effects, God's recalling them to his mind, or witnessing deeds embodied in fitting beautiful or ugly forms; he may also be admonished by divine power.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p128#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p128#2/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p128#2/r6.claim: “How could he benefit from the reminder?” denies useful remembrance because its proper time has passed; an omitted “benefit” can also be supplied, but is not needed on Alusi's analysis.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p128#2/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p128#2/r7.speaker: المعتزلة
ALUSI-FULL:v30p128#2/r7.claim: Alusi says the verse is used against the Muʿtazilite claim that reason makes acceptance of repentance obligatory: if this late remembrance is repentance, its lack of benefit challenges that claim.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p128#2/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p128#2/r8.speaker: الضحاك
ALUSI-FULL:v30p128#2/r8.claim: Al-Dahhak explicitly calls this remembrance repentance, according to Ibn Abi Hatim; an objection says the Muʿtazilites require acceptance only before the end of moral obligation.

ELMALILI:89:16-26#2/r20.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:89:16-26#2/r20.speaker: author
ELMALILI:89:16-26#2/r20.claim: Hell is brought into view and exposed to the misguided so clearly that they can no longer deny or avoid it, as stated in al-Shu‘ara.

ELMALILI:89:16-26#2/r21.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:89:16-26#2/r21.speaker: author
ELMALILI:89:16-26#2/r21.claim: The second “that day” substitutes for the preceding “when”; on that day the heedless person finally understands truths ignored in life, but too late to act.

ELMALILI:89:16-26#2/r22.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:89:16-26#2/r22.speaker: author
ELMALILI:89:16-26#2/r22.claim: Late understanding can only make the person feel punishment, loss, longing, and regret, because the chance to return and act has passed.

QUTB-ZILAL:89:23/r1.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:89:23/r1.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:89:23/r1.claim: The person who ignored the test of giving and withholding, hoarded inheritance and wealth, neglected orphans and the poor, and committed oppression will finally remember and take heed, but too late.

QUTB-ZILAL:89:23/r2.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:89:23/r2.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:89:23/r2.claim: Remembrance in the abode of recompense can no longer help; it brings only regret for losing the chance to act in worldly life.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p325/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p325/r1.speaker: طرفة
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p325/r1.claim: Tarafa's lines voice the pre-Islamic boast that wealth, noble children, and status reflect divine favor and rank.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p325/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p325/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p325/r2.claim: Quraysh, Tamim, and others asked the Prophet to expel poor believers so they might follow him; they made the same request of Abu Talib, and verse 6:52 addressed this error.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p325/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p325/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p325/r3.claim: Worldly status is no measure of merit or final recompense; earlier peoples held similar delusions and were punished, while judgment belongs to the Resurrection.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p325/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p325/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p325/r4.claim: Most commentators do not explain how the passage's argument connects to its context, apart from al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p325/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p325/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p325/r5.claim: Al-insan is grammatically generic, but its customary scope here is the disbelieving Meccans who dominate the discourse, as in several Meccan passages.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p337/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p337/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p337/r6.claim: Bringing Hell means displaying and opening it, like the cited passages about its doors and the exposed Fire; an authentic report gives its supernatural dragging.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p337/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p337/r7.speaker: ابن مسعود عن النبي
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p337/r7.claim: A report in Muslim says Hell is drawn by seventy thousand reins, each held by seventy thousand angels; the author treats afterlife events as supernatural.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p338/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p338/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p338/r1.claim: The passage mentions Hell because it warns those who ignored admonition; Paradise is also brought near, as another verse says.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p338/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p338/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p338/r2.claim: The first ‘that day’ attaches to ‘brought’; the second replaces the clause about the earth being crushed and is governed with it by ‘remember.’ Fronting stresses the time and builds suspense after a long interruption.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p338/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p338/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p338/r3.claim: ‘The human’ is the disbeliever already introduced in verse 15; it is repeated rather than pronominalized because the antecedent is distant.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p338/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p338/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p338/r4.claim: ‘Where could remembrance benefit him?’ is an interposed rhetorical question denying that a reminder can now help him.

TABATABAI:89:1-30#2/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:89:1-30#2/r4.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
TABATABAI:89:1-30#2/r4.claim: The Prophet says Hell will be led on the Day of Resurrection by seventy thousand reins held by seventy thousand angels; it would burn the heavens and earth if God did not restrain it. The report is also transmitted from Abu Saʿid and Ibn Masʿud and through a Shia chain from ʿAli.

TABATABAI:89:23-28/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:89:23-28/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:89:23-28/r1.claim: The question “how can remembrance help?” is a figure for its uselessness: on the day of recompense there is no return for repentance or good works.

TABATABAI:89:23/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:89:23/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:89:23/r2.claim: Bringing Hell means making it appear to them, as in passages where it is exposed to those who see or go astray and the veil is removed.

TABATABAI:89:23/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:89:23/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:89:23/r3.claim: At the Resurrection, people remember fully that worldly good and evil were God's test and that they fell short.

BINTSHATI:v2p157/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p157/r1.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p157/r1.claim: The continuation of the scene cites Quranic warnings that people will turn away with no protector from God.

BINTSHATI:v2p157/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p157/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
BINTSHATI:v2p157/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas says the earth is stretched like hide and widened before the gathering.

BINTSHATI:v2p157/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p157/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
BINTSHATI:v2p157/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas describes the earth stretched wide, God arriving with kneeling nations, and a herald summoning those who praised God in every condition.

BINTSHATI:v2p157/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p157/r4.speaker: أبي بن كعب
BINTSHATI:v2p157/r4.claim: Ubayy ibn Ka'b transmits from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet, a long account of people waiting, seeking intercession through prophets, and Muhammad interceding after prostration.

BINTSHATI:v2p157/r5.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p157/r5.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p157/r5.claim: The author declines to investigate these reports' chains or narrators because the Quran itself gives no hint of their details.

BINTSHATI:v2p157/r6.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p157/r6.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p157/r6.claim: Hell's arrival is personification and animation, a recurring Quranic way of depicting the afterlife; here it embodies and exposes the greatest terror.

BINTSHATI:v2p158/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p158/r1.speaker: الزمخشري
BINTSHATI:v2p158/r1.claim: Al-Zamakhshari reads the lament as proof that people had choice and were not compelled to obey or sin; the author declines the broader free-will debate.

BINTSHATI:v2p158/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p158/r2.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p158/r2.claim: The speech expresses remorse, including recognition that what has passed cannot return.

BINTSHATI:v2p158/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p158/r3.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p158/r3.claim: Anna signals distance and layta an impossible or distant wish: the deceived person longs to return and do good before punishment arrives.

CORPUSCORANICUM:89:1-5:kommentar/r5.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:1-5:kommentar/r5.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:1-5:kommentar/r5.claim: Later additions in 23–24 and 27–30 bring the afterlife dimension into the sura and help decode the enigmatic oath.

CORPUSCORANICUM:89:21-26:kommentar/r5.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:21-26:kommentar/r5.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:21-26:kommentar/r5.claim: Verses 23–24 and 27–30 are later insertions that expand the original four-verse eschatological unit and enact the oath's duality as an antithesis.

CORPUSCORANICUM:89:21-26:kommentar/r6.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:21-26:kommentar/r6.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:21-26:kommentar/r6.claim: The inserted first clause explicitly names Hell, clarifying the otherwise unspecified divine punishment of verses 25–26.

CORPUSCORANICUM:89:21-26:kommentar/r7.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:21-26:kommentar/r7.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:21-26:kommentar/r7.claim: The inserted clause in 23b–24 focuses on the human response to Hell, paralleling the worldly human responses in the secondary pair 15–16.

CORPUSCORANICUM:89:23-24:anmerkung/r1.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:23-24:anmerkung/r1.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:23-24:anmerkung/r1.claim: The pairs in verses 15–16 and 29–30 rhyme only approximately through ḏikrā and ḥayātī.

CORPUSCORANICUM:89:23-24:anmerkung/r2.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:23-24:anmerkung/r2.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:23-24:anmerkung/r2.claim: Several of the seven canonical readers use imāla for ḏikrā, making it sound closer to ḥayātī than it first appears.

CORPUSCORANICUM:89:23:anmerkung/r1.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:23:anmerkung/r1.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:23:anmerkung/r1.claim: The depiction of Hell being brought is linked to the scene in 79:36.

CORPUSCORANICUM:89:23:anmerkung/r2.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:23:anmerkung/r2.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:23:anmerkung/r2.claim: For the expression yaumaʾiḏin, the commentary points to its note on 102:8.

CORPUSCORANICUM:89:23:anmerkung/r3.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:23:anmerkung/r3.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:23:anmerkung/r3.claim: For the term Jahannam, the commentary points to 78:21.

CORPUSCORANICUM:89:23:anmerkung/r4.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:23:anmerkung/r4.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:23:anmerkung/r4.claim: Damascus, Ḥimṣ, Mecca, and Medina divide the verse after ǧahannama.

CORPUSCORANICUM:89:23:anmerkung/r5.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:23:anmerkung/r5.speaker: Neuwirth
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:23:anmerkung/r5.claim: Neuwirth accepts that verse division because verse 23 is unusually long and consists of two independent main clauses.

CORPUSCORANICUM:89:23:anmerkung/r6.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:23:anmerkung/r6.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:23:anmerkung/r6.claim: The remembrance clause is compared with 79:35, and the terms ḏikr, ḏikrā, and taḏkira are discussed at 73:19.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p297/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p297/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p297/r4.claim: The passage portrays the helplessness of people who loved wealth and failed to turn it into a means of salvation on Judgment Day.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p313/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p313/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p313/r4.claim: Paradise and Hell will also be unveiled, with Hell mentioned first because the sūrah's principal addressees are Islam's active adversaries; seeing it will bring them despair.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p313/r5.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p313/r5.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p313/r5.claim: Verse 24 explains the person's realization in verse 23: those who now dismiss warnings will regret failing to prepare for the Hereafter, but the time to amend will have passed.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:89:21/r4.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:89:21/r4.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:89:21/r4.claim: The coming of God or His command and the angels' ranks belong to the unseen, whose nature cannot be specified; believers should believe in the afterlife, accountability, and act accordingly.

QIRAAT-ER:89:23:2#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:89:23:2#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:89:23:2#1/r1.claim: A rounded transition before long ī is a prosodic adjustment with no change to root, voice, or syntax.

STUDYQURAN:89:23/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:89:23/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:89:23/r1.claim: A hadith says Hell will be brought forth with seventy thousand leashes, each pulled by seventy thousand angels.

STUDYQURAN:89:23/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:89:23/r2.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:89:23/r2.claim: People will remember their conduct, but can no longer repent or make up lost time.

STUDYQURAN:89:23/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:89:23/r4.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:89:23/r4.claim: A hadith says believers too will regret each time they remembered God in life, since that remembrance will be a source of regret on Judgment Day.
